old:
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation, showing the true change in the volume of output — the measure of growth (value vs volume).

GDP per capita divides real GDP by population — the better guide to average living standards.

GNI — GDP plus net income from abroad, such as profits sent home by citizens overseas minus income flowing out to foreign owners.

old:
The Edexcel six: technological advances; changes in relative productivity; changes in education and skills; changes in government regulations; demographic changes and migration; competition policy.

Each works by changing the quantity or quality of the factors of production. The policies that target them are supply-side policies (2.6.3).
new:
Six factors:

  • Technological advances.
  • Changes in relative productivity.
  • Changes in education and skills.
  • Changes in government regulations.
  • Demographic changes and migration.
  • Competition policy.

Each works by changing the quantity or quality of the factors of production.

The policies that target them are supply-side policies (2.6.3).

old:
Households and firms are linked by two pairs of flows. Real flows: households provide the factors of production — land, labour, capital, enterprise — and firms provide goods and services.

Money flows: firms pay income — rent, wages, interest, profit — and households return it as consumer expenditure, which becomes firms' revenue. Income circulates continuously between the two.
new:
Households and firms are linked by two pairs of flows.

Real flows: households provide the factors of production — land, labour, capital, enterprise — and firms provide goods and services.

Money flows: firms pay income — rent, wages, interest, profit — and households return it as consumer expenditure, which becomes firms' revenue.

Income circulates continuously between the two.

old: Additions of new spending that expand the flow: investment (I) — firms' spending on capital goods, sourced from the financial sector; government spending (G) — public-sector spending on state-provided goods and services; exports (X) — revenue from foreign buyers of domestic output.
new:
Additions of new spending that expand the flow:

  • Investment (I) — firms' spending on capital goods, sourced from the financial sector.
  • Government spending (G) — public-sector spending on state-provided goods and services.
  • Exports (X) — revenue from foreign buyers of domestic output.

old: Incomes not spent on domestic output, shrinking the flow: savings (S) — income placed in banks or pensions (the financial sector); taxation (T) — income paid to the government; imports (M) — spending that flows overseas. Also called leakages.
new:
Incomes not spent on domestic output, shrinking the flow:

  • Savings (S) — income placed in banks or pensions (the financial sector).
  • Taxation (T) — income paid to the government.
  • Imports (M) — spending that flows overseas.

Also called leakages.

old:
Extending the model to include the government, the financial sector and foreign trade adds flows that change the size of the circular flow: injections — investment, government spending, exports — enter it, and withdrawals — savings, taxation, imports — leave it.

The economy grows when the money entering exceeds the money leaking out.
new:
Extending the model to include the government, the financial sector and foreign trade adds flows that change the size of the circular flow:

  • Injections — investment, government spending, exports — enter it.
  • Withdrawals — savings, taxation, imports — leave it.

The economy grows when the money entering exceeds the money leaking out.

old:
The multiplier is the process by which an initial injection, such as an increase in government spending, investment, or exports, leads to a larger final increase in national income and real GDP.

The multiplier ratio k = final change in real GDP ÷ initial injection. If a £2 billion increase in government spending raises GDP by £6 billion, the multiplier is 3.
new:
The multiplier is the process by which an initial injection, such as an increase in government spending, investment, or exports, leads to a larger final increase in national income and real GDP.

The multiplier ratio k = final change in real GDP ÷ initial injection.

If a £2 billion increase in government spending raises GDP by £6 billion, the multiplier is 3.

old:
Each shows what happens to an extra pound of income: MPC — the proportion spent on domestic goods and services; MPS — the proportion saved; MPT — the proportion paid in tax; MPM — the proportion spent on imports.

MPC + MPS + MPT + MPM = 1, because every extra pound is either consumed, saved, taxed or spent on imports.
new:
Each shows what happens to an extra pound of income:

  • MPC — the proportion spent on domestic goods and services.
  • MPS — the proportion saved.
  • MPT — the proportion paid in tax.
  • MPM — the proportion spent on imports.

MPC + MPS + MPT + MPM = 1, because every extra pound is either consumed, saved, taxed or spent on imports.

old:
The trade cycle is the fluctuation in real GDP over time, with periods of boom and recession, as actual GDP rises and falls around the long-term trend rate of growth.

Four phases: boom (peak, above trend); recession (downturn — a technical recession is two consecutive quarters of negative growth); slump (trough, largest negative gap); recovery (expansion back towards trend).
new:
The trade cycle is the fluctuation in real GDP over time, with periods of boom and recession, as actual GDP rises and falls around the long-term trend rate of growth.

Four phases:

  • Boom (peak, above trend).
  • Recession (downturn — a technical recession is two consecutive quarters of negative growth).
  • Slump (trough, largest negative gap).
  • Recovery (expansion back towards trend).

old:
Boom: high and rising real GDP; low unemployment; demand-pull inflation; a positive output gap; high confidence and investment; rising tax revenue.

Recession: falling real GDP; rising unemployment; low or falling inflation; a negative output gap; low confidence and investment; falling tax revenue — which is why deficits widen in downturns.
new:
Boom

  • High and rising real GDP.
  • Low unemployment.
  • Demand-pull inflation.
  • A positive output gap.
  • High confidence and investment.
  • Rising tax revenue.

Recession

  • Falling real GDP.
  • Rising unemployment.
  • Low or falling inflation.
  • A negative output gap.
  • Low confidence and investment.
  • Falling tax revenue — which is why deficits widen in downturns.

old:
Consumers — higher real incomes and living standards, lower absolute poverty, more employment. Firms — higher demand, confidence, investment and profits. Government — rising tax receipts (income tax, corporation tax, VAT) and lower welfare spending.

Higher incomes and profits can also fund better environmental technology — growth is not automatically dirty.
new:
• Consumers — higher real incomes and living standards, lower absolute poverty, more employment.
  • Firms — higher demand, confidence, investment and profits.
  • Government — rising tax receipts (income tax, corporation tax, VAT) and lower welfare spending.

Higher incomes and profits can also fund better environmental technology — growth is not automatically dirty.

old:
Demand-pull inflation; worsened inequality when gains are uneven; environmental damage — pollution, resource depletion, biodiversity loss; worse work-life balance; a worsening current account as imports rise; congestion and housing pressure; more consumption of demerit goods.

Hence the modern debate: should governments target growth itself, or broader measures of societal well-being?
new:
• Demand-pull inflation.
  • Worsened inequality when gains are uneven.
  • Environmental damage — pollution, resource depletion, biodiversity loss.
  • A worsening current account as imports rise.
  • Worse work-life balance.
  • More consumption of demerit goods.

Hence the modern debate: should governments target growth itself, or broader measures of societal well-being?

old: Economic growth (sustainable, around 2–3%); low unemployment (near full employment, around 4–5%, allowing for frictional unemployment); low and stable inflation (CPI target of 2%); balance of payments equilibrium on the current account; balanced government budget over the cycle; greater income equality (often measured by the Gini coefficient); protection of the environment (for example net-zero commitments).
new:
• Economic growth (sustainable, around 2–3%).
  • Low unemployment (near full employment, around 4–5%, allowing for frictional unemployment).
  • Low and stable inflation (CPI target of 2%).
  • Balance of payments equilibrium on the current account.
  • Balanced government budget over the cycle.
  • Greater income equality (often measured by the Gini coefficient).
  • Protection of the environment (for example net-zero commitments).

old:
Demand-side policies are policies used by the government or central bank to shift the aggregate demand (AD) curve in order to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as low inflation, low unemployment, and economic growth.

Monetary policy — managed by the independent Bank of England: interest rates and the money supply. Fiscal policy — managed by the government: government spending (G) and taxation (T).
new:
Demand-side policies are policies used by the government or central bank to shift the aggregate demand (AD) curve in order to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as low inflation, low unemployment, and economic growth.

  • Monetary policy — managed by the independent Bank of England: interest rates and the money supply.
  • Fiscal policy — managed by the government: government spending (G) and taxation (T).

old:
A lower base rate makes borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding. Consumption rises as credit is cheaper and mortgage payments fall, freeing disposable income; investment rises as more projects clear the cheaper cost of borrowing. Both are components of AD, so AD shifts right.

Raising rates runs the chain in reverse — the standard tool for cooling inflation.
new:
A lower base rate makes borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding.

  • Consumption rises as credit is cheaper and mortgage payments fall, freeing disposable income.
  • Investment rises as more projects clear the cheaper cost of borrowing.

Both are components of AD, so AD shifts right.

Raising rates runs the chain in reverse — the standard tool for cooling inflation.

old:
Deficit: G > T — the government must borrow, adding to the national debt. Surplus: T > G — the excess can repay debt. Balanced: G = T.

Direct taxes are levied on income and profits — income tax, corporation tax, National Insurance. Indirect taxes are levied on spending — VAT and duties — and are paid via the seller.
new:
• Deficit: G > T — the government must borrow, adding to the national debt.
  • Surplus: T > G — the excess can repay debt.
  • Balanced: G = T.

Direct taxes are levied on income and profits — income tax, corporation tax, National Insurance.

Indirect taxes are levied on spending — VAT and duties — and are paid via the seller.

old:
Time lags — monetary policy can take up to two years to bite (fixed-rate mortgages delay the pass-through; investment takes time to plan). Liquidity trap — near the 0% lower bound, further cuts do little, forcing resort to QE. Asset price bubbles — cheap money can inflate housing and stock markets.

Fiscal stimulus adds a further cost: deficits accumulate into debt, constraining future policy. And any stimulus risks overshooting into inflation.
new:
• Time lags — monetary policy can take up to two years to bite (fixed-rate mortgages delay the pass-through; investment takes time to plan).
  • Liquidity trap — near the 0% lower bound, further cuts do little, forcing resort to QE.
  • Asset price bubbles — cheap money can inflate housing and stock markets.

Fiscal stimulus adds a further cost: deficits accumulate into debt, constraining future policy.

And any stimulus risks overshooting into inflation.

old:
Supply-side policies aim to increase the productive potential of the economy, shifting the LRAS curve to the right.

Market-based policies increase capacity by removing government intervention — lower taxes, deregulation, privatisation. Interventionist policies increase capacity through government spending — education, training, infrastructure.
new:
Supply-side policies aim to increase the productive potential of the economy, shifting the LRAS curve to the right.

  • Market-based policies increase capacity by removing government intervention — lower taxes, deregulation, privatisation.
  • Interventionist policies increase capacity through government spending — education, training, infrastructure.

old: Give a supply-side policy for each aim in the specification.
new: Give a supply-side policy for each aim.

old: Incentives — cut income tax so work pays (though top-rate cuts can be regressive, and some workers reduce hours instead). Competition — deregulation and privatisation, lowering barriers to entry. Labour-market reform — more flexible hiring and working arrangements. Skills — spending on education and training. Infrastructure — investment in transport, energy and digital networks.
new:
• Incentives — cut income tax so work pays (though top-rate cuts can be regressive, and some workers reduce hours instead).
  • Competition — deregulation and privatisation, lowering barriers to entry.
  • Labour-market reform — more flexible hiring and working arrangements.
  • Skills — spending on education and training.
  • Infrastructure — investment in transport, energy and digital networks.

old:
Growth vs inflation — demand-led growth pulls prices up. Growth vs the environment — more production means more emissions and resource use. Growth vs equality — gains often accrue to higher earners first. Growth vs the current account — rising incomes suck in imports.

And the classic: low unemployment vs low inflation, captured by the short-run Phillips curve.
new:
• Growth vs inflation — demand-led growth pulls prices up.
  • Growth vs the environment — more production means more emissions and resource use.
  • Growth vs equality — gains often accrue to higher earners first.
  • Growth vs the current account — rising incomes suck in imports.

And the classic: low unemployment vs low inflation, captured by the short-run Phillips curve.

old:
Monetary: higher rates curb inflation by cutting AD — but the same cut hits investment and growth. Fiscal: expansionary policy boosts short-run growth but widens the deficit and debt, constraining future policy. Supply-side: market-based reforms buy efficiency at the cost of equity, while interventionist ones reduce inequality but cost more and work slowly.

Good evaluation names the trade-off, then argues which side matters more in the given context.
